newsitem.title: USA: Where to draw the line on Net privacy.
newsitem.headline: Where to draw the line on Net privacy.

text.p: For proof that privacy is issue No. 1 with Internet users, look no further than last week's goof by America Online.

The country's largest online service had quietly altered its user terms of service -- the rules subscribers agree to abide by when they sign up -- so it could rent out members' telephone numbers to telemarketing partners such as membership buying club CUC International Inc. and TeleSave Holdings Inc., a discount phone service.

The new telemarketing scheme, which wasn't publicly announced, was to take effect July 31. But when reporters and AOL subscribers found out, it instantly made headlines. After widespread protests by customers and electronic-rights advocates, and a one-day, 2.6 percent dip in the company's stock price, AOL Chairman Steve Case capitulated and cancelled the policy. However, AOL may still make telemarketing calls for its partners, the company said.
The incident points out how seriously Internet users take their online privacy.

Selling lists of consumer names, addresses and phone numbers is the norm in the direct-marketing industry. But the Internet is held to a different standard, according to Christine Varney, outgoing Federal Trade Commission commissioner.

On the Internet, where companies such as America Online can track a person's online behaviour and match it with other demographic data, using that information "is so much more an invasion of privacy," said Varney, speaking at an electronic privacy gathering in San Francisco held the same day AOL cancelled the telemarketing plan.
That's not to say the government should step in and regulate what information companies can gather online, said Varney, who will leave her post in September to practice Internet law.

"Government solutions are burdensome and often times an invasion," she said. "We need the government to act as a floor. When it comes to children, we should have laws regarding collection of information without a parent's consent."
But regulating junk "spam" mail and other commercial uses of the Net could chill innovation and challenge freedom of speech, Varney said.
Instead, Varney and other free-market advocates support using technology to solve the privacy problem.

One solution: using software to block "cookies," Web-site technology that tracks a visitor's password, shopping purchases and other data and stores it on the person's computer hard drive for future reference. Cookie filtering programmes include Pretty Good Privacy's Cookie Cutter (http://www.pgp.com), Barefoot Productions' CookieMaster 2.0, available from ZDNet's Hotfiles shareware library (http://www.hotfiles.com), and The Limited Software's Cookie Crusher, also available from Hotfiles.

A working group of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) (http://www.ietf.org), a leading Internet industry group, is recommending changing Web browsers to automatically block cookies unless the user chooses to let them through. Currently, Netscape Navigator and Microsoft Internet Explorer browsers automatically allow cookies to be delivered unless the user changes preference settings to block them.

But by using cookie-blocking software and otherwise cloaking their identify, consumers may make going online less productive and less fun, said David Carlik, a former Internet ad executive, also speaking at the electronic-privacy meeting.

Carlik likened it to renting a car. Some people allow car-rental companies to keep personal information on file in exchange for receiving better service. Renters who don't usually have to wait in long lines and receive poorer service. It's the same on the Internet, he said.
"Privacy is important, but not as important as making life easier," Carlik said.

Another technology solution to the privacy question is encryption, using sophisticated mathematical algorithms to code and decode e-mail and other information. Encryption is at the heart of a debate between electronic-rights advocates, who favour it, and lawmakers, who want a back door into encyption programmes and controls on its export for national security reasons.

But allowing lawmakers to peek into encrypted information would be akin to letting them eavesdrop on someone's phone calls or open their postal mail, said Phil Dunkelberger, president of encryption sofware maker Pretty Good Privacy, in San Mateo, Calif., also speaking at the meeting.

"Nobody wants the government -- or a neighbour -- in their house reading their files. But (the debate) has gotten so complicated and biased that it's become hard to have a conversation about it," he said.

Even with cookie filters and encryption, consumers might not be as safe online as they believe, said Peter Neumann, a computer science and security specialist at SRI International, the Menlo Park, Calif., research centre. An enormous amount of personal data resides in Web-based directories and other online databases, all ripe for the picking for anybody bent on stealing someone else's identity.
"It's utterly trivial to perpetrate identity theft," Neumann said. "All you need are a few simple pieces of information. ... Once it's out there, there's no controlling it."
When it comes to determing the best level of privacy online, there's no simple answer, Pretty Good Privacy's Dunkelberger concluded.
"The only way around it is for people to get educated and weigh in on the issues," he said.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
